❓
Big Question
Today’s Wonder

An empty seat, a sword in a stone and a cup no one can look at all come to Camelot in one day. What can a thing stand for?

🎯
Objectives
By the end of this lesson…
🪑Symbol: I will explain what an empty seat, a sword in a stone and a veiled cup stand for.
📖Reading: I will follow the day the Holy Grail came to Camelot, using details from the chapter.
🔤Words: I will learn five words from Chapter 1.
✨Sequence: I will put the day’s marvels in order and light the new name on the Siege Perilous.
📝Writing: I will pick a knight and a moment for Quick Write 4.

🪑 Today’s Word: Symbol
Professor Lovelore names this week’s first word
Professor Lovelore Literature expert
0:52
An AI-generated character and voice.
symbol noun
A real thing in a story that stands for an idea bigger than itself.
📌 This week Green gives you three
An empty seat. A second sword in a second stone. A cup too bright to look at.
What makes someone worthy of a place that no one else can fill?
2
✏️ Daily Oral Language
Study the model, then fix the sentence.
✅ Correct model
Every Christmas, my cousin Anna visits Boston.

Names of particular people, places and holy days start with a capital letter: Christmas, Anna, Boston. The first word of a sentence does too. When two complete thoughts sit side by side, they need a full stop between them or a joining word.

🔧 Fix this one
Step 1 Tap the words that need a capital letter. 0 / 3
Step 2 Two complete thoughts run together between Camelot and every. Choose the fix.

🪶 Poetry Corner

Tennyson wrote a poem in the voice of Galahad, the young knight you meet in today’s chapter. You will read more of it over the next three lessons.

Alfred, Lord Tennyson (1809–1892)
1:00
AI voice reading, not a recording of Tennyson. Photograph: Julia Margaret Cameron, 1865, public domain (source).
🖋️ Pen: Galahad says his strength is as the strength of ten. Tap the line that tells why.
Sir Galahad
Alfred, Lord Tennyson (1842)
My good blade carves the casques of men, My tough lance thrusteth sure, My strength is as the strength of ten, Because my heart is pure. [Omitted: four stanzas] Sometimes on lonely mountain-meres I find a magic bark; I leap on board: no helmsman steers: I float till all is dark. A gentle sound, an awful light! Three angels bear the holy Grail: With folded feet, in stoles of white, On sleeping wings they sail. Ah, blessed vision! blood of God! My spirit beats her mortal bars, As down dark tides the glory slides, And star-like mingles with the stars.
casques: helmets · thrusteth: strikes forward · mountain-meres: lakes high in the mountains · bark: a small boat · helmsman: the one who steers a boat · awful: filling you with awe · stoles: long white robes like a priest’s · blood of God: in Christian belief, Christ’s blood, which the Grail held at the Last Supper · mortal bars: the limits of a human body, like the bars of a cage · mingles: mixes in

Part 1Chapter ThinkingComplete sentences, with details from the text.
